In the yard

Bulk by the yard. Stone by the pallet.

Everything loose is sold by the cubic yard out of the block bins. The hardscape sits laid out up front, where you can walk it before you buy it. Tap a heading to see what's in it.

  • Crushed grey rock in more than one size — the bins that run down the middle of the yard.
  • Rockery and landscape boulders, stacked loose at the front where a machine can reach them.
  • Feature rock for water features and focal points — the counter will walk you through the sizes.

Sizes and stock move with the season. Call the yard for what's in the bins today.

  • Red bark — the rust-colored bin two down from the gravel, the one most beds around here get topped with.
  • Darker brown bark and fines for a quieter finish.
  • Sold by the yard, loaded loose or delivered in a full load.

Three inches is the usual depth for a bed. The calculator below turns your beds into yards.

  • Screened topsoil — clean enough to top-dress a lawn and reseed straight over it.
  • Bob's Mix — their own blend, sold under its own name off its own bin sign. You won't find it at a big box store, because it isn't one.
  • Garden and raised-bed soil by the yard.

Bringing a trailer? Wet soil is heavy — tell the counter what you're towing with.

  • Sand in the pale bins at the end of the row.
  • Pea gravel — the small round stone, the one people come in for by the bucket.
  • Gravel by the yard for base and drainage work.

Contractors on the Orting–Kapowsin corridor pass the gate on the way to the job. Loading takes a few minutes.

  • Pavers and wall block, stacked on pallets and built into finished samples you can stand next to.
  • Flagstone by the pallet — the big irregular slabs along the fence line.
  • Fire pit kits and bench stone, sitting assembled in the display area so you can see the real size.
  • Basalt columns and steps for a hillside or a stairway.

This is the part worth driving out for. Photos flatten stone — standing next to it doesn't.

Getting it home

Bring a truck, or we'll bring the truck.

Two ways it leaves the yard, and both of them start with a phone call or a pull-in.

01

Loaded at the bin

Back the truck or trailer up to the bin you want and it goes in by the bucket. Tell the counter your yardage — or the number the calculator just gave you — and they'll take it from there.

02

Delivered by the yard

Orders go out on their own truck and get dropped where you want them, not at the end of the driveway. Ask what a run to your address costs when you call it in.

Their one-of-one

Bob's Mix

One bin in the row doesn't have a grade on the sign. It has a name. Every other pile out there is a spec you could buy anywhere — this one is theirs, blended here, sold under their own logo, and you can't get it at a big-box lot.

Where it ends up

It leaves here in a pile. It doesn't stay one.

Two jobs that started as a scoop out of these bins.

Get a price

Three steps and you're loaded.

  1. Measure the space

    Length, width, and how deep you want it. That's all the yard needs to price a load.

  2. Call it in

    Say which material and how many yards. If you're not sure, describe the job — they do this all day.

  3. Pull in, or pick a delivery day

    Come get loaded at the bin, or have it dropped where the work is.
